propositions.text: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large knife robbed a variety store at night.
The robbery was caught by the store's security camera.

paragraphs.summary: A man wearing a blue Halloween mask and holding a large knife robbed a store; security camera recorded it, court states.

propositions.text: Police found a blue Halloween mask, a large knife, and a plastic cover from the store's cash register the next morning.
DNA on the blue mask matched only Marty David O'Brien with a probability of 1 in 33 billion.

paragraphs.summary: Police found mask, knife, and cash register cover; DNA on mask matched only Marty David O'Brien, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O'Brien was charged and convicted of three offences, including robbery.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. O'Brien was charged and convicted of three offences including robbery, court states.

propositions.text: At trial, nine witnesses testified before Justice Murphy without a jury.
Investigating officer briefly referenced Mr. O'Brien's prior criminal record and conduct during testimony.
Defence did not object to this evidence and used it in cross-examination of the officer.

paragraphs.summary: At trial, nine witnesses testified; investigating officer mentioned O'Brien's prior record; defence used this evidence in cross-examination, court states.

propositions.text: Only defence counsel referred to Mr. O'Brien's reputation as a 'known offender' in closing submissions.
The Crown and trial judge made no mention of the character evidence in closing or reasons.

paragraphs.summary: Only defence counsel mentioned O'Brien's reputation in closing; Crown and judge did not mention character evidence, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O'Brien did not testify and defence called no evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Mr. O'Brien did not testify and defence called no evidence, court states.

propositions.text: Mr. O'Brien appealed to Nova Scotia Court of Appeal on ground that verdict was unreasonable.
Court clerk asked counsel to address character evidence issue though it was not raised in notice of appeal or factum.

paragraphs.summary: O'Brien appealed on unreasonableness; court clerk requested addressing character evidence though not raised by appellant, court states.

propositions.text: Crown acknowledged trial judge erred by not excluding or qualifying character evidence.
Crown argued error was not serious and curative proviso should apply under Criminal Code s. 686(1)(b)(iii).

paragraphs.summary: Crown acknowledged trial judge's error on character evidence but argued it was not serious and curative proviso applies, respondent argues.

propositions.text: All three judges found verdict not unreasonable.
Majority held trial judge made serious error allowing character evidence to be heard.
Trial judge did not disabuse himself of character evidence or recognize it could not be considered.
Crown did not prove judge was not influenced by prejudicial evidence; curative proviso not available.
Appeal allowed and new trial ordered.

paragraphs.summary: Majority of Court of Appeal found serious error in character evidence use, no proof judge was uninfluenced, appeal allowed and new trial ordered, earlier_decision_maker finds.

propositions.text: Dissenting judge would have dismissed appeal.
Error in hearing propensity evidence was not serious and caused no miscarriage of justice.
Trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence, excluding improper character testimony.
Curative proviso was available and dissenting judge shared this view.

paragraphs.summary: Dissenting judge found error harmless, trial judge relied on DNA evidence only, curative proviso applies, dissenting judge finds.

propositions.text: Whether trial judge's error in hearing bad character evidence and failure to address it was harmless or outside curative proviso.

paragraphs.summary: Issue is whether trial judge's error on bad character evidence was harmless or outside curative proviso, court states.

propositions.text: At trial, only issue was identification.
Trial judge cautioned about identification evidence and found circumstantial evidence strongly connected blue mask to robbery beyond reasonable doubt.
Investigating officer's character evidence played no role in this finding.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge found circumstantial evidence strongly connected mask to robbery; character evidence played no role, court finds.

propositions.text: Trial judge stated identification of accused to mask depended entirely on DNA evidence.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge stated identification depended entirely on DNA evidence, court finds.

propositions.text: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence clearly tied Mr. O'Brien to the mask beyond reasonable doubt.
DNA evidence established accused's identity as robber beyond reasonable doubt.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge concluded DNA evidence clearly tied O'Brien to mask and established identity beyond reasonable doubt, court finds.

propositions.text: Propensity evidence played no part in convictions.
Trial judge expressly relied entirely on DNA evidence to identify Mr. O'Brien.
When trial judge independently arrives at conclusion without inadmissible evidence, no unfairness or miscarriage of justice arises (R. v. Leaney).

paragraphs.summary: Propensity evidence played no part; trial judge relied on DNA only; independent conclusions without inadmissible evidence cause no unfairness, court finds.

propositions.text: Trial judge's statement of relying entirely on DNA means he did not rely on character evidence.
Imputing reliance on character evidence despite contrary reasons creates unchartable appellate review.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge's reliance on DNA excludes character evidence; imputing otherwise creates unchartable appellate review, court finds.

propositions.text: Trial judge must show how result was reached but need not itemize every issue or thought process.
Trial judges should be reviewed on what they say, not speculative imagination (R. v. Sheppard).
Trial judges should not be held to abstract standard of perfection.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judges must show reasoning but not every thought; review based on reasons not speculation; no abstract perfection standard, court states.

propositions.text: Trial judge's chain of fact, law and logic was impeccable with no subconscious subversion.

paragraphs.summary: Trial judge's reasoning was impeccable with no subconscious error, court finds.

propositions.text: Admission of improper character evidence was harmless error causing no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice.

paragraphs.summary: Admission of improper character evidence was harmless error causing no miscarriage, court concludes.

propositions.text: Appeal allowed and convictions restored.

paragraphs.summary: Appeal allowed and convictions restored, court concludes.

propositions.text: The Crown relies on DNA evidence to uphold convictions from a trial deemed unfair by Nova Scotia Court of Appeal judges.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown relies on DNA evidence to uphold convictions from an unfair trial.

propositions.text: The respondent was convicted as the masked robber with identification as the only live issue.
No evidence linked the respondent to the crime except DNA on masks found near the scene.
Unfairness arose because police told the court about the respondent's unrelated criminal reputation.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the respondent's conviction was based on DNA and unfair police evidence about his reputation.

propositions.text: The trial judge admitted propensity evidence without comment and did not recognize its unfairness.
Trial judges may misapply the law, necessitating appellate review.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge admitted unfair propensity evidence and notes appellate courts are needed for such errors.

propositions.text: The respondent, sentenced to over six years, deserves assurance the trial judge recognized propensity evidence danger.
The trial judge's reasons do not assure he consciously set aside the propensity evidence danger.

paragraphs.summary: The court concludes the respondent deserves assurance the trial judge recognized propensity evidence danger, but reasons do not show this.

propositions.text: A majority finds the trial judge's use of 'entirely' on DNA evidence renders trial unfairness harmless.
The court disagrees, saying this ignores trial context and DNA evidence problems causing wrongful convictions.
The Crown must show no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice despite unfair trial under s. 686(1)(b)(iii) Criminal Code.
The court would dismiss the appeal, finding the Crown has not discharged its burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court disagrees with the majority that DNA evidence alone cures unfairness and would dismiss the appeal as the Crown failed its burden.

propositions.text: The Crown's trial evidence portrayed the respondent as a bad person likely to commit the robbery.
Beveridge J.A. found the inadmissible evidence was extensive and showed the accused was known to police for similar offences.
R. v. Suzack established the Crown cannot prove guilt by showing misconduct unrelated to the charged offence.
Police Sgt. Blakeney testified the respondent was thought involved in multiple incidents and was known as an active criminal.
The police evidence of criminality was unrelated to the charged offences.
The officer spoke to the respondent who denied involvement; later DNA orders were issued and monitored.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts Crown's bad character evidence, police testimony, and legal rule forbidding such evidence to prove guilt.

propositions.text: Defence counsel did not object and trial judge did not intervene or show concern about the improper evidence.
Both majority and minority in the court below found the bad character evidence inadmissible and trial unfair.
R. v. Handy states prejudice is risk of unfocused trial and wrongful conviction from propensity evidence undermining presumption of innocence.
Beveridge J.A. noted the use of propensity evidence was not inadvertent.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes no objection was made but lower courts found bad character evidence inadmissible and unfair, citing R. v. Handy.

propositions.text: Identification rested on two strands: the red car and DNA evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court states identification evidence included the red car and DNA evidence.

propositions.text: A red car was seen near the scene; respondent's ex-girlfriend owned a red car he had access to during their relationship.
The witness did not confirm the car was the same or continuing access at the robbery time.
The trial judge correctly found the red car evidence unhelpful.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the red car evidence unhelpful and uncertain regarding the respondent's access or identification.

propositions.text: DNA was recovered from two masks; one matched the respondent's DNA.
DNA match does not prove guilt but shows contact with the mask like a fingerprint.
The Crown acknowledged DNA evidence alone does not establish the respondent was the masked robber.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains DNA evidence matched the respondent but does not alone prove guilt, acknowledged by the Crown.

propositions.text: The trial judge relied entirely on DNA evidence to link the respondent to the mask used in the robbery.
An inferential leap is needed from DNA contact to actual use of the mask in the robbery.
DNA evidence alone does not bridge the gap without police information about the respondent's criminal background.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge relied solely on DNA but an inferential leap and police evidence were needed to link the respondent to the robbery.

propositions.text: Section 686(1)(b)(iii) allows upholding conviction despite trial judge's legal error if no substantial wrong or miscarriage of justice occurred.
The legal error was admitting evidence portraying the respondent as a career criminal likely to commit the robbery.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the curative proviso allows upholding conviction despite error admitting bad character evidence.

propositions.text: Curative proviso applies only if trial outcome would necessarily be the same despite the error (Colpitts).
The Crown bears the onus to establish this high standard (R. v. Jolivet, Khan, Van).

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the curative proviso requires the Crown to prove the trial outcome would be the same despite error.

propositions.text: Curative proviso applies if Crown shows on balance of probabilities the error was harmless or evidence is overwhelming (Khan, Jolivet, Van).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the curative proviso applies if the Crown proves harmless error or overwhelming evidence on balance of probabilities.

propositions.text: Relying on trial judge's silence or use of 'entirely' is insufficient to apply the curative proviso.
The word 'entirely' likely reflects no other identification evidence, not distancing from inadmissible evidence.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the trial judge's silence and word 'entirely' insufficient to apply the curative proviso.

propositions.text: The court's concern does not impute flawed reasoning based on speculation.
The Crown bears the burden to show improper evidence was harmless; Abella J.'s reasoning reverses this burden.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the Crown bears the burden to prove harmlessness and rejects reasoning that reverses this burden.

propositions.text: The respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the trial judge to accept DNA evidence uncritically.
The respondent submits DNA evidence impact could be dangerously exaggerated by knowledge of his proclivities.

paragraphs.summary: The respondent argues bad character evidence prejudiced the trial judge to overvalue DNA evidence.

propositions.text: The Crown says the trial judge was unaffected by bad character evidence because he did not mention it in reasons.
Beveridge J.A. noted the trial judge gave no indication of awareness of the problem during evidence or reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The Crown argues the trial judge was unaffected by bad character evidence, but Beveridge J.A. found no indication of awareness.

propositions.text: The Court of Appeal majority declined the curative proviso partly because no other evidence linked respondent to the crime.
R. v. Mars states fingerprint evidence's ability to connect accused depends on other evidence linking accused to crime.
R. v. Samuels distinguished Mars where other evidence linked accused to crime.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Court of Appeal majority declined the curative proviso due to lack of other evidence, citing Mars and Samuels.

propositions.text: Beveridge J.A. noted the Crown conceded DNA on mask alone does not establish accused's culpability.
DNA presence is equivalent to a fingerprint; small amounts can persist for years and transfer by handling.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Beveridge J.A. recorded the Crown's concession that DNA alone does not prove culpability and explained DNA transfer facts.

propositions.text: Disagree with Abella J. that admission of evidence blackening respondent's character was harmless
Trial judge's failure to address problematic police evidence is a significant deficiency
Crown argues trial judges are presumed to know the law
Important deficiencies in trial reasons cannot be excused by presumption that trial judges know the law, per R. v. Sheppard

paragraphs.summary: The court finds admission of bad character evidence was not harmless, trial judge's failure to address police evidence is a deficiency, rejects Crown's presumption argument citing R. v. Sheppard.

propositions.text: Crown invokes R. v. Leaney where inadmissible police opinion evidence was deemed surplusage
In Leaney, trial judge found police opinion evidence unnecessary and surplusage
Difference between Leaney's inadmissible opinion evidence and prejudicial bad character evidence here
Officers' testimony in Leaney was unobjectionable in content, problem was source; here information itself is objectionable

paragraphs.summary: The Crown relies on Leaney; court distinguishes Leaney's surplusage police opinion evidence from prejudicial bad character evidence here.

propositions.text: Crown should not benefit from curative proviso as trial judge showed no awareness of police testimony problem
In R. v. Rahm, trial judge understood bad character evidence inadmissible if character not in issue
No such understanding evident in trial reasons here

paragraphs.summary: Court finds no curative proviso benefit as trial judge unaware of police testimony problem, unlike Rahm where judge understood bad character evidence rules.

propositions.text: Trial judge's error of law cannot be dismissed as harmless
Respondent entitled to a new trial unless harmlessness can be affirmatively found

paragraphs.summary: Court concludes trial judge's error is not harmless and respondent deserves new trial unless harmlessness is proven.

propositions.text: Curative proviso may apply if case against accused is overwhelming despite non-harmless error

paragraphs.summary: Court states curative proviso applies if case against accused is overwhelming despite error.

propositions.text: In Court of Appeal, Crown did not argue case was so strong that conviction was inevitable
Dissenting judge also did not suggest case was overwhelming
Court agrees these concessions were correct

paragraphs.summary: Court notes Crown and dissenting judge conceded case was not overwhelming; court agrees.

propositions.text: Denying new trial based on appellate conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence is exceptional

paragraphs.summary: Court states denying new trial on conjecture of harmless error or overwhelming evidence is exceptional.

propositions.text: R. v. Trochym sets high burden on Crown to invoke curative proviso, higher than proof beyond reasonable doubt
Appellate standard requires evidence so overwhelming conviction is inevitable
Higher standard reflects difficulty of retroactively assessing excluded evidence impact
Crown cannot establish case against respondent was overwhelming

paragraphs.summary: Court cites Trochym for high curative proviso burden and finds Crown cannot prove overwhelming case against respondent.

propositions.text: Agrees with majority below that curative proviso does not apply
Would dismiss appeal
Appeal allowed with Binnie and LeBel JJ. dissenting
Solicitors for appellant and respondent named

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees with majority below that curative proviso does not apply and would dismiss appeal; appeal allowed with dissent noted.
